patient.name: Callum O'Brien
patient.setting: GP surgery, then the urology 2-week-wait clinic
patient.complaint: A painless lump in his right testicle, noticed in the shower 6 weeks ago
background: Mild back ache for a month

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young man and a scrotal lump: painless, hard, intratesticular and not transilluminating means cancer; the tumour markers and age separate seminoma from teratoma.

points: Callum, 27: **painless** lump in the right testis for 6 weeks.
Dull ache in his lower back for a month.
No fever, no dysuria, no trauma.

steps.lead: Callum's lump is **hard, craggy and painless**, and the torch test shows it does not transilluminate.
At 27 he sits right in the **15 to 35** age band for germ cell tumours.
Callum's childhood **undescended testis** is his biggest risk factor, even though it was fixed.

points: Lump is **within** the testis; you cannot feel the testis separately.
You **can** get above it; cord normal.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: A **painless, hard, intratesticular** lump that does not transilluminate in a young man is testicular cancer until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: Callum's lump is **in** the testis, not around it (hydrocele) or above and separate (epididymal cyst).
Which germ cell tumour? Callum's age and markers will decide between **seminoma** and a **non-seminoma**.

steps.text: Gynaecomastia with a testicular lump: think **hCG-secreting** germ cell tumour raising the oestrogen to androgen ratio.

steps.lead: Callum's back ache could be **para-aortic node** disease: these tumours spread there first, not to the inguinal nodes.

steps.text: Testicular cancer drains to the **para-aortic** nodes (the testis develops near the kidney). Inguinal nodes drain the **scrotal skin**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (scrotal ultrasound), 'Which confirms the diagnosis?' (radical inguinal orchidectomy) and questions on AFP, beta-hCG and LDH.

o: Percutaneous needle biopsy of the testis
steps.r: **Scrotal ultrasound** first: it confirms the mass is intratesticular. A needle through the scrotum risks seeding the tumour.

steps.lead: Callum's ultrasound shows a 3 cm **intratesticular** mass, and the bloods include all three tumour markers.

steps.title: Callum's tumour markers
steps.text: A raised **AFP** rules out a pure seminoma; this is a **non-seminomatous** germ cell tumour.

visual.title: Callum's AFP
visual.label: Callum 410
visual.caption: AFP is never produced by pure seminoma. Any rise means non-seminoma elements.

steps.lead: Callum's diagnosis is confirmed by **radical inguinal orchidectomy**: the whole testis gives the histology.
After orchidectomy, Callum is staged with **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis**.

visual.title: Chest imaging at staging
visual.caption: Rounded nodules in both lungs: lung metastases, alongside para-aortic nodes on CT.

steps.text: Never biopsy a testicular mass **through the scrotum**: it can seed tumour into scrotal lymphatics. Diagnosis is by inguinal orchidectomy.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (2WW referral, then radical inguinal orchidectomy) and the next step after histology (BEP for non-seminoma, radiotherapy or carboplatin for seminoma).

steps.q: What should the GP do today?
steps.r: Any **suspicious testicular mass** needs a 2-week-wait referral. Antibiotics for a painless lump only delays the diagnosis.

steps.lead: Callum's hard, painless lump meets **NICE NG12** for 2-week-wait referral.
Within days Callum has a **radical inguinal orchidectomy**: diagnosis and first treatment in one operation.

steps.text: Offer **sperm banking** before orchidectomy and chemotherapy, and a testicular prosthesis at surgery.

steps.lead: Callum has a non-seminoma with spread, so he gets **BEP**: bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin.

visual.title: Callum's markers on treatment
visual.caption: Markers falling to normal shows response. A later rise means relapse.

steps.lead: Callum's follow-up is **surveillance**: regular tumour markers and CT scans for years.

science.exam: Science questions ask where germ cell tumours come from, why cryptorchidism raises risk, why seminoma is radiosensitive and which cells make AFP and hCG.

steps.lead: Callum's tumour began in the **germinal epithelium** of his seminiferous tubules.
Callum's orchidopexy did not remove the risk: early **heat** damage to germ cells had already happened.
If Callum's tumour had been a seminoma, its **uniform, primordial-germ-cell-like** cells would make it very radiosensitive.
Callum's tumour has mixed, **less differentiated** elements, which is why it grew and spread quickly.

steps.r: **AFP** comes from yolk sac elements. Syncytiotrophoblast cells make beta-hCG.

steps.lead: Callum's AFP proves yolk sac elements; his hCG shows **syncytiotrophoblastic** cells too.

mcq.r: **Radical inguinal orchidectomy**, which also gives histology.

mcq.r: **Syncytiotrophoblastic** cells, seen in some seminomas and in choriocarcinoma.

technique.stem: A 30 year old man has noticed a painless swelling of his left testis over 2 months. The testis feels heavy. Examination shows a hard, irregular mass within the left testis. It is possible to get above the swelling. It does not transilluminate. The epididymis feels normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a scrotal lump: where is it, how does it feel and does it light up?

clues: hard, irregular mass within the left testis
steps.x: Painless, hard, intratesticular, non-transilluminating, scrotal (can get above it).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Testicular tumour.**

elim: A cyst is fluctuant, transilluminates and lies separate from the testis.
A hydrocele is soft and transilluminates, with the testis inside the fluid.
You cannot get above a hernia; this swelling is confined to the scrotum.
A varicocele is a soft 'bag of worms' above the testis.

steps.x: **D. Testicular tumour.** Rule: hard + within the testis + no transillumination = cancer until proven otherwise.

technique.stem: A 26 year old man has a painless, hard mass in his right testis. Scrotal ultrasound shows a 2.5 cm solid intratesticular lesion. His AFP is 85 kU/L (<10) and beta-hCG 40 IU/L (<5). The urologist needs to establish the histological diagnosis.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Fine needle aspiration through the scrotum

steps.x: The question asks for histology: how do you get tissue safely?
A solid testicular mass with raised markers is cancer; the tissue must come out via the groin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Radical inguinal orchidectomy**, the gold standard.

elim: CT stages the disease; it does not give histology.
Trans-scrotal sampling risks seeding tumour into scrotal lymphatics.
MRI images the mass but does not give histology.
A solid intratesticular mass with raised markers needs action now.

steps.x: **D. Radical inguinal orchidectomy.** Never needle a testis through the scrotum.

technique.stem: A 39 year old man had a radical inguinal orchidectomy for a right testicular mass. Histology shows a pure seminoma. His AFP is normal. CT shows small-volume para-aortic lymphadenopathy. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?

steps.x: Next treatment after orchidectomy: decide seminoma or non-seminoma.
Seminoma with nodal spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Seminoma is chemo- and radiosensitive: **radiotherapy or carboplatin**.

elim: Anti-androgens treat prostate cancer, not germ cell tumours.
GnRH agonists are for prostate cancer.
Tamoxifen is a breast cancer drug.
He has nodal spread, so further treatment is needed.

steps.x: **B. Carboplatin chemotherapy.** Seminoma = radiotherapy or carboplatin; non-seminoma = BEP.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has testicular cancer. At 3 years old he had an orchidopexy for a left undescended testis. The tumour is in the left testis.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism linking his history to the tumour?
o: Higher intra-abdominal temperature impairing germ cell maturation
Ischaemia of the testis from the surgery
Raised oestrogen exposure in utero only

steps.x: A mechanism question linking a past history to a tumour.

clues: The tumour is in the left testis
steps.x: Cryptorchidism raises risk even after surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The undescended testis was exposed to **higher temperature**, impairing germ cell maturation.

elim: That is not how cryptorchidism raises risk.
Infection does not cause germ cell tumours.
Surgery does not cause the tumour; risk remains despite it.
Not the mechanism given for cryptorchidism.

steps.x: **C. Higher intra-abdominal temperature.** Risk persists after orchidopexy.

practice.stem: A 28 year old man has a 2 month history of a painless swelling in his right testis. There is no history of trauma or urinary symptoms. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. There is a hard, craggy mass in the right testis that does not transilluminate. The left testis is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A painless, hard, craggy testicular mass that does not transilluminate in a young man is a germ cell tumour. Hydroceles and cysts transilluminate.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a scrotal lump in a young man.
Painless, hard, craggy, non-transilluminating, in the age group.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Testicular germ cell tumour.**

elim: A cyst is fluctuant, transilluminates and is separate from the testis.
Infection is painful with fever and urinary symptoms.
A hydrocele transilluminates.
A varicocele is a soft 'bag of worms', usually left-sided.

steps.x: **D. Testicular germ cell tumour.**

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has a slowly enlarging painless lump in his left testis for 4 months. Examination shows a firm, smooth mass within the testis that does not transilluminate. Ultrasound shows a homogeneous intratesticular mass. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A slow-growing tumour in a man in his late 30s with a normal AFP is seminoma. Teratoma and yolk sac tumours raise AFP.

steps.x: Diagnosis of the tumour type: use age and markers.
Older end of the range, slow-growing, AFP normal, hCG only slightly up.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Seminoma.**

elim: A non-seminoma: AFP is usually raised.
A rare sex cord tumour, often with hormonal effects; markers are normal.
Teratomas present younger and raise AFP or hCG.
Yolk sac tumours make AFP, which is normal here.

steps.x: **C. Seminoma.** AFP normal = no yolk sac elements.

practice.stem: A 21 year old man has a 3 week history of a rapidly enlarging lump in his right testis and cough. There is a hard, irregular intratesticular mass. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 120/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray (see item resources)
visual.caption: Multiple rounded opacities in both lungs.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A raised AFP excludes pure seminoma. A fast-growing tumour in a young man with lung metastases is a non-seminoma.

steps.x: Diagnosis of the tumour type: AFP is the decider.
Young, fast-growing, very high AFP and hCG, probable lung spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Non-seminomatous germ cell tumour** (e.g. teratoma or mixed).

elim: Infection is painful and febrile, with normal markers.
Sex cord tumours do not make AFP.
Pure seminoma never raises AFP and grows slowly.
Lymphoma affects men over 60.

steps.x: **C. Non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.**

practice.stem: A 25 year old man has 2 months of tender breast enlargement. He takes no medicines and does not use anabolic steroids or cannabis. Examination shows bilateral gynaecomastia and a painless hard lump in the left testis. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his breast enlargement?
practice.e: A germ cell tumour secreting hCG raises the oestrogen:androgen ratio and causes gynaecomastia. Always examine the testes in a young man with gynaecomastia.

steps.x: A cause question: link the breasts to the testis.

clues: painless hard lump in the left testis
steps.x: Gynaecomastia plus a hard testicular lump and raised hCG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An hCG-secreting **testicular germ cell tumour** raising the oestrogen:androgen ratio.

elim: He denies using them.
He denies using it.
Klinefelter gives small, soft testes from puberty, not a hard lump.
He takes no medicines.

steps.x: **E. Testicular germ cell tumour.**

practice.stem: A 29 year old man has a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour of the right testis. He has had a dull central back ache for 6 weeks. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely site of lymph node spread?
practice.e: Testicular cancer spreads first to the para-aortic (retroperitoneal) nodes, which can cause back pain. Inguinal nodes drain scrotal skin.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question on spread.
Testicular lymphatics follow the testicular vessels back to the kidney level.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Para-aortic (retroperitoneal) lymph nodes.**

elim: These drain the arm and breast.
Inguinal nodes drain the scrotal skin, not the testis.
These can be involved later, not first.
Left supraclavicular (Virchow's) nodes are a late, distant site.

steps.x: **D. Para-aortic lymph nodes.** Back pain is the clue.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man has a painless lump in his right testis. As a baby his right testis had not descended and he had an orchidopexy at age 2. He has no other medical history. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 124/82 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular mass.
practice.q: Which is the most important risk factor in his history?
practice.e: Cryptorchidism is the key risk factor and remains so after orchidopexy. Family history, previous testicular cancer and infertility are others.

steps.x: A risk-factor question: what in his past raises risk?
A previously undescended testis, now with a solid mass.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cryptorchidism**, which still raises risk after orchidopexy.

elim: Hernia repair is not a recognised risk factor.
He has no history of mumps; it is not a recognised testicular cancer risk factor.
Trauma often draws attention to a lump but does not cause it.
A varicocele is not a testicular cancer risk factor.

steps.x: **A. Cryptorchidism.**

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has noticed a painless lump in his left testis for 3 weeks. Examination shows a hard nodule that seems to be within the testis but the examination is difficult. He has been referred urgently to urology.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Scrotal ultrasound is first-line and shows an intratesticular mass. Trans-scrotal biopsy is contraindicated.

steps.x: Initial investigation of a scrotal lump.

clues: within the testis but the examination is difficult
steps.x: The key question is: is it intratesticular and solid?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Scrotal ultrasound.**

elim: CT is for staging after the diagnosis.
MRI is not first-line for a scrotal lump.
Never biopsy through the scrotum: it seeds tumour.
PSA is a prostate marker.

steps.x: **D. Scrotal ultrasound.** Plus AFP, beta-hCG and LDH.

practice.stem: A 27 year old man has had a radical inguinal orchidectomy. Histology shows a mixed germ cell tumour. His AFP and beta-hCG remain raised 2 weeks after surgery. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to stage his disease?
practice.e: Testicular cancer is staged with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis to look for para-aortic node and lung spread.

steps.x: A staging question after the diagnosis is made.
Persistent markers suggest spread; stage the nodes and lungs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.**

elim: Bone is not a usual early site and bone scan is not routine staging.
Lymphangiography is obsolete.
The other testis is not the staging question.
Ultrasound images the retroperitoneum and lungs poorly.

steps.x: **B. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.**

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has a painless, hard lump in his left testis. Scrotal ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular mass. His AFP is 70 kU/L (<10). CT shows no spread. He has banked sperm. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: First-line management is radical inguinal orchidectomy, which also gives histology. A scrotal approach risks spread.

steps.x: Initial management of a solid testicular mass.
Testicular cancer: remove the testis via the groin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Radical inguinal orchidectomy.**

elim: Chemotherapy follows orchidectomy, guided by histology and stage.
This is a tumour, not infection.
A solid mass with raised AFP needs treatment now.
The scrotal approach risks seeding the scrotal lymphatics.

steps.x: **C. Radical inguinal orchidectomy.**

practice.stem: A 23 year old man has had a radical inguinal orchidectomy for a teratoma. CT shows para-aortic lymph node metastases. His AFP is 640 kU/L (<10). His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
practice.e: Non-seminomatous tumours with spread are treated with BEP chemotherapy. Radiotherapy and carboplatin alone are seminoma options.

steps.x: Next treatment after orchidectomy: non-seminoma with spread.
Metastatic non-seminoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Combination chemotherapy: **BEP** (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin).

elim: Anti-androgens are for prostate cancer.
Radiotherapy suits seminoma, not non-seminoma.
Carboplatin alone is a seminoma option.
He has metastatic disease and needs treatment.

steps.x: **A. BEP chemotherapy.**

practice.stem: A 35 year old man completed treatment for a testicular seminoma 3 months ago. He feels well. His tumour markers are normal and CT shows no residual disease. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Discharge to GP with no follow-up
Surveillance with tumour markers and imaging
practice.e: Follow-up after testicular cancer is surveillance with tumour markers and imaging to detect relapse early.

steps.x: Long-term management after treatment.
Relapse is detected by markers and CT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Surveillance** with tumour markers and imaging.

elim: PSA is a prostate marker.
Relapse can occur; he needs surveillance.
Removing the healthy testis is not indicated.
Bone is not the usual relapse site.

steps.x: **E. Surveillance with tumour markers and imaging.**

practice.stem: A 22 year old man has a testicular germ cell tumour. His AFP is 900 kU/L (<10). Histology after orchidectomy shows several tissue types.
practice.q: Which tumour component is most likely producing the AFP?
practice.e: AFP is produced by yolk sac elements and never by pure seminoma. Beta-hCG comes from syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells.

steps.x: A science question: which cells make which marker?
AFP means yolk sac elements in a mixed tumour.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Yolk sac elements.**

elim: Leydig cells make testosterone.
Pure seminoma never produces AFP.
Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis and do not make AFP.
These produce beta-hCG.

steps.x: **E. Yolk sac elements.** hCG = syncytiotrophoblast.

prompts.q: What is testicular cancer, who gets it and what are the risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: young man + undescended testis.

points.why: Commonest solid cancer in young men.

points.p: Family history, previous testicular cancer, infertility

prompts.q: Describe the classic testicular cancer lump.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: painless and does not transilluminate.

points.why: Pain points towards infection or torsion.
A cyst is separate from the testis.
Gynaecomastia from a raised oestrogen:androgen ratio.

prompts.q: How do seminoma and non-seminoma differ?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: AFP is the decider.

points.p: Seminoma: ~50%, slow, stays in testis longer
Non-seminoma: yolk sac, embryonal, mixed, teratoma

points.why: AFP is never raised in pure seminoma.

prompts.q: Where does testicular cancer spread, and what is the emergency?

points.why: Endometrial and ovarian cancer also spread there.

points.p: Spinal cord compression: severe back pain or neurology

prompts.q: How do you tell a hydrocele, epididymal cyst and varicocele from a tumour?

points.p: Hydrocele: soft, fluid, transilluminates, testis within it
Epididymal cyst: fluctuant, separate from testis, head of epididymis
Varicocele: left-sided, nutcracker effect, may signal renal cancer
points.why: Left renal vein compressed by aorta and SMA.

prompts.q: What are the first-line investigations and tumour markers?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ultrasound first, never a scrotal needle.

prompts.q: What confirms the diagnosis and how is it staged?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: orchidectomy is both diagnosis and treatment.

points.p: Gold standard: radical inguinal orchidectomy for histology
Staging: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
points.why: Looks for nodes and lung spread.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: refer, remove, then treat by type.

prompts.q: Why does cryptorchidism raise risk, and why is seminoma radiosensitive?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: temperature and cell uniformity.

points.p: Germ cell tumours arise from germinal epithelium of seminiferous tubules
Higher intra-abdominal temperature impairs germ cell maturation
Seminoma: uniform cells like primordial germ cells

glossary.germ cell tumour: A tumour arising from sperm-forming cells; most testicular cancers.
glossary.seminoma: A slow-growing, radiosensitive germ cell tumour; about half of testicular cancers.
glossary.non-seminomatous germ cell tumour: Germ cell tumours other than seminoma, e.g. teratoma, yolk sac, embryonal; more aggressive.
glossary.teratoma: A germ cell tumour containing several tissue types; grows and spreads faster than seminoma.
glossary.yolk sac tumour: A non-seminomatous germ cell tumour that produces AFP.
glossary.embryonal carcinoma: An aggressive non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.
glossary.choriocarcinoma: A germ cell tumour of trophoblast cells that produces very high hCG.
glossary.cryptorchidism: Undescended testis; the main testicular cancer risk factor.
glossary.orchidopexy: Surgery to bring an undescended testis down and fix it in the scrotum.
glossary.radical inguinal orchidectomy: Removing the testis and cord through a groin incision; diagnoses and treats testicular cancer.
glossary.transilluminate: Light passing through a swelling, showing it contains fluid.
glossary.intratesticular: Within the substance of the testis.
glossary.AFP: Alpha-fetoprotein: a tumour marker made by yolk sac elements; never raised in pure seminoma.
glossary.beta-hCG: Beta human chorionic gonadotrophin: a tumour marker made by syncytiotrophoblast cells.
glossary.hCG: Human chorionic gonadotrophin; raised in some testicular tumours.
glossary.LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase: a non-specific marker of tumour burden.
glossary.para-aortic lymph nodes: Retroperitoneal nodes beside the aorta; the first site of testicular cancer spread.
glossary.retroperitoneal: Behind the peritoneum, at the back of the abdomen.
glossary.hydrocele: Fluid around the testis giving a soft swelling that transilluminates.
glossary.epididymal cyst: A benign fluid-filled swelling in the epididymis, separate from the testis.
glossary.varicocele: Dilated veins of the pampiniform plexus, a 'bag of worms', usually left-sided.
glossary.nutcracker effect: Compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and SMA.
glossary.BEP: Bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin: chemotherapy for non-seminoma.
glossary.bleomycin: A chemotherapy drug in BEP; can cause lung fibrosis.
glossary.cisplatin: A platinum chemotherapy drug in BEP.
glossary.carboplatin: A platinum chemotherapy drug used for seminoma.
glossary.seminiferous tubules: Tubules in the testis where sperm are made.
glossary.germinal epithelium: The sperm-producing lining of the seminiferous tubules.
glossary.sperm banking: Freezing sperm before treatment that may affect fertility.
glossary.2-week-wait: NICE urgent referral pathway for suspected cancer.
glossary.NG12: NICE guideline on recognising and referring suspected cancer.
